title: Identity versus explicit rule wording on the existing firm pilot
provenance: A small curated pilot built from primary corporate disclosures. Records are short factual paraphrases, not raw registry extracts. Labels were authored from these disclosures before model responses; they are independent of the evaluated model but have not had independent human adjudication. Null labels mark unsupported or inapplicable relations. Cases within a corporate family are correlated. Original test responses have already been inspected; this fixture is for development and regression diagnostics, not fresh validation.
split_policy: Development: GE and Tesla/NUMMI. Test: HP, IBM/Kyndryl, Meta, and Lordstown/Foxconn. No prompt or threshold tuning after model responses.

arms.identity: Original identity prefix with rich records.
arms.rule: Explicit supplied rule with identical rich records.

rules.legal_entity: Match the same legal corporation, including a documented name change or trade name. Distinct incorporated parents, subsidiaries, buyers and sellers do not match. A transferred business or a shared factory does not establish legal identity. Use the entity described by each record, not a former owner.
rules.corporate_group: Match records belonging to the same ultimate corporate group at their respective as_of dates. A corporation and its controlled subsidiary count. Renaming the continuing parent does not change the group. After a spin-off or sale, use the new controller; a former parent or a non-controlling minority stake does not establish common control. Business units inherit their parent group.
rules.physical_site: Match the same identifiable physical factory or facility across records, even when its owner, operator, name or product changes. Different physical locations do not match even when they share a company. This rule concerns the site, not legal entity or corporate ownership.
rules.operating_business: Match the same specifically described operating business or production program continuing over time, including its transfer to a new corporation or contractor. A rename alone preserves the operation. Different divisions or production programs do not match just because they share a parent, broad industry or reused building. A whole diversified company and one of its businesses are not automatically identical.
